items.prompt: Funnel view -> signup -> purchase with a 7-day window. One person views on day 0, signs up on day 5 and purchases on day 9. How far do they get?
items.answer: Step 2: the purchase is 9 days after the view that anchors the window
distractors: Step 3, as the purchase lands within 7 days of the day-5 signup
Step 3, because the window only bounds the gap between neighbouring steps
Step 1 only; the signup resets the anchor, so the chain breaks
items.explanation: computeFunnel compares every later step with anchor + windowMs, and the anchor is the step-1 timestamp (funnel.ts:58, 62). The window is measured from step 1, not from the previous step.

items.prompt: With a 7-day window, the last step happens at exactly anchor + 7 days, to the millisecond. Does it count?
items.answer: Yes; the comparison is t <= anchor + windowMs, so the edge is inside
distractors: No, the window is half-open and ends just before anchor + 7 days
Yes, but only for the last step; earlier ones use a strict t < anchor + windowMs
It depends on rounding, since timestamps are bucketed to whole days
items.explanation: funnel.ts:62 uses t <= anchor + windowMs. The guide states the edge is inclusive: exactly anchor + window counts, one millisecond later does not.

items.prompt: A person signs up (step 2) on day 0 and views the page (step 1) on day 1, then does nothing else. What does the funnel count?
items.answer: They count at step 1 only; the earlier signup is ignored
distractors: They complete both steps, because order is ignored inside the window
They are not counted at all: an out-of-order chain discards the person
They count at step 2, as the signup still falls within 7 days of the view
items.explanation: At level 0 only a step-1 event can match (funnel.ts:56-61); the day-0 signup is skipped. After the view anchors at day 1 there is no later signup, so the person stays at step 1. Ordered-with-gaps means B ... A leaves you stuck at step 1.

items.prompt: Window 7 days. A person views on day 0, views again on day 6 and signs up on day 8. Does the signup count?
items.answer: No, because the anchor stays at the earliest view, so the window closed
distractors: Yes, the day-6 view re-anchors the window to start on day 6
Yes: any step-1 event within 7 days of the signup will do
No; a repeated step-1 event disqualifies the person entirely
items.explanation: The anchor is set only while level === 0 (funnel.ts:56-59), so the second view changes nothing; day 8 > 0 + 7 days fails the check at line 62. The person is counted at step 1, not dropped.

items.prompt: A funnel is broken down by $browser. A person's first step-1 event was on Firefox and every later event on Chrome. Where are they counted?
items.answer: In the Firefox group, with all their events, as their first view was Firefox
distractors: In both groups, split by the browser property that each separate event carries
In the Chrome group, since most of their events carry that browser
In "(none)", as the browser property differs across their events
items.explanation: computeFunnelBreakdown labels each person once, from the property on their FIRST step-1 event (funnel.ts:100-108), then puts all of that person's events into that group. "(none)" is only used when the property is missing.

items.prompt: Why does bucket() put the flagKey inside the hashed string, next to the distinctId?
items.answer: So that two flags give uncorrelated splits instead of reusing one
distractors: So that a user can be moved between variants by editing the key
It is only a cache key; the hash itself reads the distinctId only
To make the hash slower, as a defence against bucket guessing
items.explanation: bucket hashes `${flagKey}:${salt}:${distinctId}` (bucketing.ts:42). Leaving the flagKey out would give every experiment the same split; the chi-square and Pearson property tests exist to catch that.

items.prompt: A flag ramps from 10% to 20% rollout. What happens to the users who were already inside the 10%?
items.answer: They stay in, since their rollout draw is unchanged and still under 0.2
distractors: They are reshuffled, and about half of them drop back out of the rollout
They are removed until the next deploy writes a fresh assignment table
They keep the flag but get a new variant from the next variant draw
items.explanation: The rollout gate is bucket(key, id, "rollout") >= rolloutPercentage / 100 (evaluate.ts:40-41). The draw depends only on the key, the salt and the user, so anyone below 0.1 is also below 0.2. The variant draw uses its own salt and does not change either.

items.prompt: An enabled flag has targeting that this user fails, and the user's rollout draw is also outside the percentage. Which reason does evaluateFlag return?
items.answer: "not_targeted": targeting runs before the rollout draw
distractors: "out_of_rollout", since the rollout gate always has the final word
"disabled": a failed predicate turns the flag off for them
"rollout", with the control variant picked by weight
items.explanation: evaluateFlag returns in order: disabled, then not_targeted (evaluate.ts:36-38), then out_of_rollout (line 41-43). A user who fails targeting never reaches the rollout draw.

items.prompt: In the 1000 A/A experiments of the peeking simulation, what false-positive rate does "check after every 100 samples, stop at p < 0.05" produce?
items.answer: About 26%: one null experiment in four called a winner
distractors: About 5%, the same alpha a single fixed-horizon look gives
About 50%, as half of the null experiments drift past p < 0.05 at some look
Zero; the A/A design cannot produce a significant difference
items.explanation: The table in peeking.md gives ~26% for peeking against ~4.7% for a fixed horizon. Every "win" in an A/A test is a false positive by construction, so the true lift is zero but noise still crosses the line.

items.prompt: computeExperimentResult runs a z-test and a confidence interval on the lift. Which standard error does each one use?
items.answer: A pooled SE for the z-test; per-arm own variance for the lift CI
distractors: Pooled for both, because the null hypothesis assumes equal rates in each arm
Unpooled for both: each of the 2 arms keeps its own variance
Separate variances in the test statistic, a shared rate for the interval
items.explanation: twoProportionZTest pools the two rates under the null (results.ts:50-51). The lift CI uses each proportion's own variance (seUnpooled, lines 70-73) because it describes the estimated difference.

items.prompt: A WRITE key is revoked. How long can it keep authenticating POST /e on an API instance that resolved it a moment ago?
items.answer: Up to 60 seconds, the TTL of the hash-to-key cache
distractors: Not at all; revocation busts the hot-path cache straight away
Until the next deploy, since keys are cached for the process lifetime
Up to 24 hours, the interval of the sampled lastUsedAt write
items.explanation: The resolver caches each hash -> key mapping with ttlMs defaulting to 60_000 (resolver.ts:38-39, 63). ADR-0003 names this the "undead key" window; an instant cache-bust on revoke is deferred.

items.prompt: A sampled query reads 400 matching events in a 10% sample. What does formatEstimate show?
items.answer: ~4,000 ±9%, the count scaled up by the sample rate, with its 95% band
distractors: ~400 ±5%, the raw observed count shown with a 5% error band
~4,000 exactly, because 400 clears the 30-event reliability floor
~40,000 ±1%: the estimate scales by the square of the sample rate
items.explanation: estimate = round(400 / 0.1) = 4000; se = sqrt(400 * 0.9) / 0.1 ≈ 189.7; ci95 = 1.96 * se ≈ 372, about 9.3% of 4000 (sampling.ts:24-39). The floor only decides reliable; it never drops the ± sign.

items.front: The five rules of Pulse's funnel contract
items.back: 1) Step 1 anchors at the person's earliest step-1 event. 2) The window is measured from step 1, not the previous step. 3) Ordered with gaps: other events may fall between steps, but B before A does not count. 4) The window edge is inclusive. 5) Same-timestamp steps advance in recorded order.

items.front: Pulse's two API key types and what each may do
items.back: WRITE (pw_live_...): public, shipped in page source, append only. SECRET (ps_live_...): server-side only, append + read. Stored as sha256 hash + identifiable prefix; the plaintext is shown once. Resolving proves a key is valid; keyCan proves it is allowed.

items.front: How does the live SSE tail treat a slow client, and why is that the opposite of ingest?
items.back: Each client has a bounded ring buffer (default 100); on overflow it drops the OLDEST frame and counts the drop ("N skipped"). Ingest promises never drop (at-least-once, durable); a live tail promises fresh. Two surfaces, opposite correctness contracts.

items.front: The three experiment result states, and why one is worded carefully
items.back: collecting / significant / "no effect detected". Never "no effect": reaching the horizon without significance only means no effect large enough to detect was found, not that the variants are equivalent (that needs an equivalence/TOST design).

items.prompt: ADR-0002 keeps events on Postgres until an exit criterion is crossed. Which of these is one of its three written criteria?
items.answer: A trends/funnel query over ~50M events exceeding ~2 s p95
distractors: The Event table passing ~50 GB on disk for a single project
Insert p95 exceeding ~2 s once ingest reaches ~500 events/sec
A funnel query over ~5M events exceeding ~200 ms p95 for a day
items.explanation: ADR-0002 lines 21-26 list exactly three: sustained ingest above ~2,000 events/sec driving insert p95 above 50 ms; a trends/funnel query over > ~50M events exceeding ~2 s p95; and the events table dominating DB size/vacuum/backup so OLTP metadata is harmed. There is no raw-size threshold, and the other numbers are mixed up from the real ones.

items.prompt: ADR-0002 leaves the Postgres Event table with a single btree on (projectId, ts): no partitioning, no BRIN, no columnar layout. Why?
items.answer: Optimizing it now would blunt the planned S07 migration lesson
distractors: Partitioning needs a Postgres version the course does not ship
Extra indexes would break the dedupe on the unique uuid column
BRIN indexes cannot serve the GROUP BY that trends depend on
items.explanation: ADR-0002 lines 40-41: the Event table is deliberately under-optimized, and optimizing it now would blunt the S07 lesson, where the team drives Pulse across the exit criteria and migrates. The ADR gives no version, dedupe or BRIN-capability reason.

items.prompt: Pulse's SDK runs every public entry point inside a never-throw guard and can report swallowed errors via onError. What does ADR-0004 add about that reporter?
items.answer: The reporting call is wrapped too, so a broken reporter can't throw
distractors: The reporter is called only in development builds, never on live pages
The reporter rethrows after logging, so the host page can see the error
The reporter batches errors and sends them along with the next flush
items.explanation: ADR-0004 lines 14-16: errors are swallowed and optionally reported via onError, and the reporting is itself wrapped, so a broken reporter can't re-break the page; a bug in analytics must never take down checkout. Rethrowing would break the first principle, and nothing limits the reporter to development or batches it.

items.prompt: ADR-0004 says the event uuid is minted in the browser at capture time. What goes wrong if it were minted downstream instead?
items.answer: A network retry would become a duplicate nothing can collapse
distractors: Two browsers could mint the same id and overwrite each other
The beacon path could not deliver an event without a header
The consumer would need a second lookup to find the person id
items.explanation: ADR-0004 lines 20-22: the uuid is the idempotency key the whole pipeline relies on (S04 dedupes on it, S07 backfill stays idempotent because of it); mint it downstream and a network retry becomes an uncollapsible duplicate, because the retried send would get a fresh id. Collisions, beacon headers and person lookups are not the stated risk.

items.prompt: ADR-0004 derives every SDK principle from one ordering of priorities. What is it, and why?
items.answer: Page safety > delivery > size > features; a throw costs more than a gap
distractors: Delivery > page safety > size > features; a lost event is unrecoverable
Size > page safety > delivery > features; the bundle budget is enforced
Page safety > size > delivery > features; the script must load quickly
items.explanation: ADR-0004 lines 34-36: the failure modes are asymmetric, since a dropped event is a data gap while a thrown exception is a customer outage and a churned account, so the order is don't break the page > deliver the event > be small > be featureful. Size is enforced in CI but ranks third, below delivery.

items.prompt: Pulse's auto-pageview patches the host page's history API. Which three properties does ADR-0004 require of that patch?
items.answer: It composes with the original, is idempotent, and is reversible
distractors: It replaces the original, is lazy, and is removed after one call
It wraps the original in a Proxy, is async, and is sandboxed
It runs before the original, is cached, and is never torn down
items.explanation: ADR-0004 lines 28-29: good-citizen monkey-patching composes with the original (call it first, return its result), is idempotent (no double-patch), and is reversible (teardown restores it exactly). It neither replaces the original nor stays installed forever.

items.prompt: Under ADR-0005's rule "place correctness where state already lives; keep the hot path dumb", where do dedup, enrichment and batching run?
items.answer: In the stream consumer, next to the database and the batch
distractors: In the ingest handler, before the event is put on the stream
In the browser SDK, before an event is ever sent to ingest
In the query layer, when a trend is read from the event store
items.explanation: ADR-0005 lines 37-39: the hot path does the least possible (validate + append), and everything stateful (dedup against a unique index, enrichment, batching) happens in the consumer, where the database and the batch already are. Ingest stays dumb, the SDK only mints ids, and query time is not where dedup lives.

items.prompt: ADR-0005 accepts that a consumer which crashes after inserting a batch but before XACK will see those entries redelivered. What makes that redelivery harmless?
items.answer: An idempotent apply: a unique uuid plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
distractors: The consumer XACKs each entry before inserting it into Postgres
Redis drops a redelivered entry whose id it has already seen
The SDK stops resending once ingest has answered with a 202
items.explanation: ADR-0005 lines 41-44: Redis Streams gives at-least-once, so redelivery after a crash between insert and XACK is the contract, not a bug to engineer away in the transport. The apply is made idempotent (unique uuid + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), and at-least-once delivery plus idempotent apply is effectively exactly-once. Acking before inserting would lose events on a crash, Redis does not dedupe redeliveries, and the SDK is not involved.

items.prompt: Pulse freezes personId onto each event row at write time (ADR-0006). When two persons are later merged, what changes?
items.answer: Mappings move to the survivor; event rows are never rewritten
distractors: The old event rows get their personId updated to the survivor
Both persons' events are copied into one new combined person
The frozen ids are recomputed by a nightly backfill of events
items.explanation: ADR-0006 lines 17-20: the event log is immutable and identity is a view over it via the mapping table, so a merge fixes the future (new lookups resolve to the survivor) while the past stays exactly as recorded. The consumer's identify (apps/consumer/src/identity.ts lines 101-117) remaps the loser's distinct ids to the winner, folds the loser's properties into the winner, deletes the loser person and re-primes the cache; it never updates an event row. No combined person is created and no backfill recomputes frozen ids.

items.prompt: How does ADR-0006 make an identify merge safe under concurrency and under replay?
items.answer: A per-user-id advisory lock, and the oldest person always wins
distractors: A table-wide lock, and the person with more events always wins
An optimistic version check, and the newest person always wins
A per-device lock, and the identified person always wins merges
items.explanation: ADR-0006 lines 22-26: the merge runs under a lock keyed on the user id (pg_advisory_xact_lock in prod), serializing concurrent identifies for that user, and the oldest person wins, which is deterministic, so a replayed identify is idempotent. Create-on-first-sight takes the lock only on its create path, so the common paths stay lock-free.

items.prompt: ADR-0006 declines cross-device probabilistic matching "probably forever". What reason does it give?
items.answer: A wrong guess silently corrupts the count of how many users
distractors: Matching models are too slow to run on the write path today
Fingerprinting devices breaks the browser privacy rules
The merge lock cannot be held across two separate devices
items.explanation: ADR-0006 lines 48-50: guessing that two ids are the same person silently corrupts "how many users?", the one number analytics must not lie about. Speed, privacy rules and lock scope are not the stated reason.

items.prompt: ADR-0007 publishes the losing options. Partitioned Postgres with rollups did ~3.1 s on some queries. Why was it still rejected?
items.answer: Rollups only answer questions named in advance, not ad-hoc filters
distractors: Rollups double the write load, so ingest at 5k/s fell further behind
Rollups need a nightly rebuild, so trends were always a day out of date
Rollups cannot count distinct persons, only raw totals of events
items.explanation: ADR-0007 lines 21 and 25-27: partitioning + rollups got ~3.1 s on rollup-able queries but ~9 s on arbitrary-filter distinct, because rollups can only precompute the questions you named in advance, and the product's superpower is arbitrary filters and breakdowns. The table records improved ingest for that option, and no nightly-rebuild claim is made.

items.prompt: The ClickHouse events table orders by (projectId, name, ts, uuid). Why does ADR-0007 put uuid last?
items.answer: So ReplacingMergeTree can collapse exact re-deliveries at merge
distractors: So a query can look up one event by uuid without a full scan
So uuid becomes the partition key for each monthly partition
So ClickHouse enforces a unique index on uuid at insert time
items.explanation: ADR-0007 lines 35-37: (projectId, name, ts) leads because nearly every insight filters on them, and uuid is last so ReplacingMergeTree can collapse exact re-deliveries. Lines 41-43: no unique index exists in ClickHouse; dedupe happens eventually at merge, plus an in-memory insert-window set in the consumer. Partitioning is by toYYYYMM(ts).

items.front: Redis Streams terms and their Kafka equivalents (ADR-0005 concept map)
items.back: XADD = produce to a topic (ingest appends an event). Consumer group = consumer group (each entry goes to one consumer). Stream entry id = offset (position/ordering). XACK = commit offset (mark an entry done). XAUTOCLAIM = partition reassignment/rebalance (rescue a dead consumer's stuck entries). XLEN/backlog = lag. Dead-letter stream = dead-letter topic (poison events, out of the main flow).

items.front: Pulse SDK: bundle budget and the events it loses on purpose
items.back: Zero runtime dependencies; the gzipped script-tag build must stay under 6 KB, enforced in CI by the SDK's budget script, packages/sdk/scripts/check-size.mjs (about 2.1 KB today). Lost by design: events in private mode without persistence, a hard crash mid-batch, and overflow drops. Completeness is traded for safety and size, and the ADR says so.

items.front: How Pulse counts distinct users on ClickHouse (ADR-0007)
items.back: uniq() (HyperLogLog) replaces exact count(distinct) for scale, with documented error bounds and golden tests that carry a defined tolerance; uniqExact is still available when exactness is worth the cost.

items.front: ADR-0008's grid for compute-on-read vs precompute
items.back: Three axes. Output size: compute when small; precompute when small and reused by many callers. Scan cost: compute when tolerable per request; precompute when high and paid repeatedly. Freshness need: compute when analysts want it live; precompute when minutes/hours of staleness is acceptable. Rule: precompute is a debt against freshness and correctness, taken on only when frequency x scan cost justifies it.

items.front: Sprint 13 audit: the six ways evidence was gathered
items.back: 1) Chaos harness: loadgen emitting duplicate, reordered and clock-skewed events (1970 and 2031) at 500 evt/s for 2 min. 2) SDK outage sim: 503s for 10 minutes with 200 simulated tabs, arrival rate sampled per second through recovery. 3) Write-key abuse probe: one key replayed at 5,000 evt/s from one origin. 4) PII sweep of a 10k-event sample and the logs. 5) Share-token probe: reuse after 90 days plus sequential-prefix enumeration. 6) pnpm audit + gitleaks over full history.

items.front: Sprint 13 remediation map: severities, fixes and the three adversaries
items.back: P1: F1 SDK retry herd, F2 client timestamps, F3 deletion (a person-delete API plus a completeness test), and a chaos suite made a permanent CI stage for F1 and F2. P2: F4 share tokens (expiry, revocation, enumeration monitor), F5 rate limit, F6 PII. P3: F7 CI gates (gitleaks plus dependency gates). Three adversaries recur: the network (F1, F5), the clock (F2) and the law (F3, F4, F6).

items.front: Why a future Kafka move would be cheap for Pulse (ADR-0012)
items.back: The EventStream port (S04) makes the transport injectable: a KafkaEventStream implementing the same interface is the shape of the move, and no code outside the index.ts entries assumes Redis. ADR-0005's concept map means the team already reasons in Kafka terms, so it is a transport swap, not a re-education. Lesson: the migration you prepared for and didn't need is preparation, not waste.

items.prompt: In the delivered consumer with EVENTS_PRIMARY=ch and DUAL_WRITE off, processNewBatch inserts a 50-event batch and then XACKs it. Where are those 50 events at the moment of the XACK?
items.answer: In the column store's in-memory buffer, not yet in ClickHouse
distractors: In ClickHouse, as insert awaits the write before the XACK runs
In Postgres, which stays the source of truth until the cutover
In the pending entries list, until the next flush acks them all
items.explanation: apps/consumer/src/index.ts lines 35-41: with EVENTS_PRIMARY "ch" there is no Postgres store, and the column store is a BufferedColumnStore wrapping the ClickHouse store. worker.ts lines 89-96 await columnStore.insert(good) and then XACK. BufferedColumnStore.insert (columnstore.ts lines 112-115) only pushes fresh uuids into an in-memory buffer and flushes when it reaches maxRows, 10,000 by default; nothing else in the consumer calls flush. So the 50 events are acknowledged while they exist only in process memory, Postgres is not written in this mode, and the XACK has already removed them from the pending entries list.
